passages.happening:
Paul is astonished at what the believers have been doing. “If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!” (verse 1).

He reminds them of what they will one day do. “Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases?” (verse 2). They will even judge angels. How much more the matters of this life (verse 3).

So why take everyday disputes to people who have no standing in the church (verse 4)? “I say this to your shame. Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?” (verse 5). Instead, brother sues brother, in front of unbelievers (verse 6).

Then Paul goes further. “The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?” (verse 7). Worse, some of them are the ones doing the cheating, even to their own brothers (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Corinth was a Roman colony, and its courts worked by Roman law. Paul is speaking of civil cases, disputes over property, money and business, which one person brought against another. He calls them ‘trivial cases’ and ‘everyday matters’ (verses 2 and 4).

In those courts, wealth and rank counted for a great deal. Historians of Roman law have shown that people of high standing had large advantages, and that it was very hard for a person of low standing to bring a case against a social superior and win. Going to court was also a public contest for honour. So the lawsuits in Corinth were most likely brought by believers of some means, against other believers, perhaps poorer ones. A church that taught that ‘not many’ of them were powerful (1:26) was using the city's power games against its own members.

Jewish communities living among Gentiles often settled their disputes among themselves, rather than before Gentile judges. Paul expects the church to be able to do the same. Surely, in a church so proud of its wisdom, someone is wise enough to settle a quarrel between brothers? The irony would not be lost on them.

‘The saints will judge the world’ draws on a Jewish hope that God's people would share in the judgment at the end of the age. If they are to share in that, a quarrel about money is small.

‘Why not rather be wronged?’ would have sounded very strange in Corinth, where you defended your honour and your rights in public. It sounds strange today too.
passages.ot:
The hope that God's holy people will share in judgment comes from Daniel. In his vision, judgment is given for the saints: “until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom” (Daniel 7:22).

Israel was told to settle disputes among its own people with fair judges. Moses charged them, “Hear the disputes between your brothers, and judge fairly between a man and his brother” (Deuteronomy 1:16). Proverbs warns against rushing to law: “do not bring hastily to court” (Proverbs 25:8).

‘Why not rather be wronged?’ follows the teaching of Jesus: “if someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:40). Jesus also said, “Reconcile quickly with your adversary, while you are still on the way to court” (Matthew 5:25).
passages.hard:
Does this passage forbid a Christian ever to go to court, or to report a crime?

No. Paul is speaking of everyday civil disputes between believers, over money, property and business: ‘trivial cases’, in his words. He is not speaking of crimes. Nothing here tells anyone to keep a crime hidden, or to settle it quietly inside the church.

This must be said plainly, because this passage has been misused. Abuse and other crimes are to be reported to the police and the proper authorities. Paul himself calls those who govern “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). A church must never use these verses to keep someone who has been harmed from going to the police, or to protect someone who has done harm. Paul's anger in this chapter is aimed at the strong who cheated the weak, not at the weak who sought help.

Paul himself used the Roman courts when he needed to. He appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and he claimed his rights as a citizen (Acts 22:25).

Christians differ on how far ‘Why not rather be wronged?’ reaches. Some hold that a believer should never sue another believer. Others think going to law can be right as a last step, when a church cannot settle a matter or when others must be protected. Many churches encourage mediation, where trusted people help both sides settle a dispute. All take Paul's main point: believers should be ready to lose for the sake of peace, and the strong must never use the law to crush the weak.
passages.asks: Paul asks whether you would rather be wronged than win. Ask whether there is a dispute in your life where you care more about getting what you are owed than about the other person. Ask, too, whether you have ever used your strength, money or position to get your way over someone weaker. And if you have been harmed by a crime, Paul is not asking you to keep quiet.

passages.t: ‘And that is what some of you were’
passages.happening:
“Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God?” (verse 9). Paul warns them not to be fooled.

Then he gives a list. “Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God” (verses 9-10).

The next sentence changes everything. “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The list comes straight after Paul's words about lawsuits and cheating, and it begins where that left off. The word for ‘wicked’ in verse 9 is the same word as ‘the unrighteous’ in verse 1, the judges the believers had been running to. Paul is saying: do not live like the people whose courts you use.

Lists of vices like this were a common form in Jewish and Greek moral teaching, and hearers knew the form. This one mixes sins of the body with sins of greed and of the tongue. Thieves, the greedy, swindlers and verbal abusers sit in the same list as adulterers. In a chapter that began with believers cheating one another in court, no one in the room could hear it and feel safe.

‘Inherit the kingdom’ means to receive the life of God's coming kingdom as a child receives an inheritance. Paul is not saying that anyone who has ever done one of these things is shut out. The next verse says the opposite. He is warning against a life given over to them, as if they did not matter.

Then verse 11. ‘That is what some of you were.’ The church in Corinth was made of people with these very pasts. Paul gives three verbs, each something God did. Washed: made clean. Sanctified: set apart for God. Justified: declared right with God. All three are past tense. They have already happened, ‘in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God’.

‘Justified’ is a courtroom word. It fits a passage that began with lawsuits. The believers who were suing for their rights had already been acquitted in God's court, not by their own case but in Christ's name.
passages.ot:
Two words in the list point back to the law of Moses. The second word in the phrase ‘men who submit to or perform homosexual acts’ is the Greek arsenokoitai. Many scholars think it was formed from the words of the Greek translation of Leviticus, which in the Berean Standard Bible reads, “You must not lie with a man as with a woman; that is an abomination” (Leviticus 18:22), and again, “If a man lies with a man as with a woman, they have both committed an abomination” (Leviticus 20:13). The same law also forbids adultery and idolatry, and requires honesty in trade (Leviticus 19:35-36).

The picture of being washed clean comes from the prophets. God promised through Ezekiel, “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols” (Ezekiel 36:25). Through Isaiah God said, “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18).

Paul later writes of the same washing: “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).
passages.hard:
What does Paul say in verses 9 and 10, and how do Christians read it?

Paul gives a list of those who “will not inherit the kingdom of God” (verse 9). It names the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, verbal abusers and swindlers. These notes state that plainly and do not soften it.

The phrase ‘men who submit to or perform homosexual acts’ joins two Greek words. The first, malakoi, means literally ‘soft ones’. The Gospels use it of fine, soft clothing (Matthew 11:8). In Paul's world it was used of men thought unmanly, and often of the passive partner in sex between men. The second, arsenokoitai, is rare. In the New Testament it appears only here and in 1 Timothy 1:10, and no clear use of it before Paul is known. It joins the Greek words for ‘male’ and ‘bed’. The Berean Standard Bible renders the two words together, with ‘submit to’ and ‘perform’ standing for the passive and the active partner.

Christians read the passage in more than one way. The historic reading of the church, and still the reading of most churches today, is that Paul speaks of same-sex sexual acts as such. On this reading the second word points back to the law of Leviticus, which speaks of any man lying with a male, and Paul's teaching rests on God's creation of humanity as male and female (Genesis 1:27). Some Christians read it differently. They hold that the two words point to particular practices of Paul's world, which they see as marked by exploitation, such as men's sexual use of boys, of slaves or of prostitutes, so that Paul was not speaking of faithful, committed same-sex relationships. Those who hold the historic reading answer that the law of Leviticus is general, and that Paul grounds sexual ethics in creation, not in particular abuses. These notes set out both readings. Faithful Christians disagree here, and these notes take no side.

Three things are plain on any reading. First, the list also names the greedy, drunkards, thieves, verbal abusers and swindlers, so that no reader stands outside it. Second, Paul's very next words are grace: “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed” (verse 11). The church is a company of the forgiven, not of the flawless. Third, nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.

If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Read the list in verses 9 and 10 slowly, and stop at the words that describe you, or once did: greed, drunkenness, cheating, cruel words, sexual sin. Ask which of them you excuse in yourself while you notice them in others. Then read verse 11 again, slowly. ‘But you were washed.’ Ask whether you believe that of yourself, and whether you believe it of the people you find hardest to love.

passages.t: ‘Everything is permissible for me’: the body is for the Lord
passages.happening:
Paul now quotes some sayings that were going round the church, and answers them.

“‘Everything is permissible for me,’ but not everything is beneficial” (verse 12). And again: “‘Everything is permissible for me,’ but I will not be mastered by anything” (verse 12).

“‘Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,’ but God will destroy them both” (verse 13). Then Paul's own answer: “The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” (verse 13).

He gives the reason. “By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The Berean Standard Bible puts ‘Everything is permissible for me’ and ‘Food for the stomach and the stomach for food’ in quotation marks. Greek manuscripts had no quotation marks, so this is a translator's judgment. Many think Paul is quoting slogans the Corinthians used, and then correcting them. The first may have begun as a twisted form of Paul's own teaching that believers are free from the law of Moses. The Corinthians had turned it into ‘I can do whatever I like’.

The second slogan seems to have argued like this. Food is for the stomach, and one day both will pass away. So what we do with our bodies does not touch the soul. Many Greeks thought of the body as a shell for the soul, a lesser thing. From there some concluded that bodily appetites, including sex, did not matter.

Paul answers each slogan without throwing out what was true in it. Yes, believers are free. But not everything is good for you, and freedom that makes you a slave to your appetites is not freedom at all. Yes, food and the stomach will pass. But the body is not a throwaway shell. It is ‘for the Lord’, and God will raise it, as he raised Jesus.

That is the heart of Paul's answer. The resurrection of the body means the body matters. What you do with it, you do as a person, before God.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament never treats the body as a mere shell. God formed the first human from the dust and breathed life into him, and the man became a living being (Genesis 2:7). A psalm praises God for the body he made: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:14).

The teaching of Jesus stands behind ‘food for the stomach’ too. He taught that food does not make a person unclean, because it goes into the stomach and out again; what defiles is what comes from the heart, including sexual immorality (Mark 7:18-21). The Corinthians took the first half and dropped the second.

Paul says the same about freedom in another letter: “For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Galatians 5:13).
passages.asks: ‘Everything is permissible’ is still a slogan people live by. Ask what you tell yourself when you want to do something you know is not good for you. Then ask Paul's two questions: Is it beneficial? Is it mastering me? What would it mean to treat your body as ‘for the Lord’?

passages.t: ‘Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit’
passages.happening:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never!” (verse 15).

Paul explains: a man who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her, for Scripture says, “The two will become one flesh” (verse 16). “But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit” (verse 17).

“Flee from sexual immorality” (verse 18). Every other sin is outside the body, Paul says, but sexual sin is a sin against one's own body.

“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
In the Roman world prostitution was legal and widespread. It was not counted a disgrace for a man to go to a prostitute, if he did not overdo it. Many prostitutes were slaves, put to that work by their owners, with no say in it at all. In a port city like Corinth, sailors and traders came and went. For some men in the church, this was simply what men did.

Corinth is often said to have had a thousand temple prostitutes. That claim comes from the geographer Strabo, who seems to have been describing the older Greek city destroyed in 146 BC, and many historians doubt it. Paul's warning does not need it. Ordinary prostitution was everywhere.

Paul's answer is not first a rule. It is about belonging. Believers' bodies are ‘members of Christ’, parts of his body. To join them to a prostitute is to treat what belongs to Christ as if it did not.

‘You were bought at a price’ would have been heard against the slave market. A slave who was bought belonged to a new master. The price, though Paul does not name it here, is Christ's death. Believers belong to him, body and all.

In 3:16 Paul said the church together is God's temple. Here the ‘your’ in ‘your body’ is plural, but ‘body’ is singular, and most readers take it of each believer's body. Each person's body is a shrine where God's Spirit lives. In a city full of temples, that was a striking thing to say about a slave's or a dock worker's body.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). For Paul, sex joins whole persons. It cannot be spiritually neutral.

‘Flee’ recalls Joseph, who, when his master's wife grabbed him, “escaped and ran outside” (Genesis 39:12). Proverbs warns against the forbidden woman: “Her feet go down to death” (Proverbs 5:5).

‘Bought at a price’ echoes God's rescue of Israel. God redeemed his people from slavery in Egypt: “With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed” (Exodus 15:13). Through Isaiah he says, “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine” (Isaiah 43:1). Peter writes that believers were redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).
passages.hard:
Human trafficking is the buying, selling or holding of people for forced work or for sex. It is evil, and it still happens today. Many of the prostitutes of Paul's world were slaves with no choice at all. Paul's words here are aimed at the men who used them, not at them.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. ‘You are not your own; you were bought at a price’ is good news for you too: in Christ you belong to the one who gave himself for you, and to no one else. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And a word for anyone who carries shame from sexual sin of their own. Verse 11 still stands over this whole chapter: ‘But you were washed’. Paul's command is to flee, and Christ's gift is to wash.
passages.asks: Paul says your body belongs to the Lord, and the Spirit lives in it. Ask how that would change the way you think about your body: what you do with it, how you care for it, how you speak about it. Then ask what it would mean, this week, to glorify God with your body.
